prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting architecture learned to pick DONE straight away (episode length 1.0, no placements). The untrained trace shows why: this world mirrors actions left to right. Every placement lands at column X-1-x (counting the whole footprint), while rows are unchanged. For example, '1x1 at row 7, col 2' filled col 5, and '1x2 at col 6' filled cols 1 and 0. The observation itself is not mirrored, since the target as observed matches the design. A convolutional head that scores an anchor using features at the same (y,x) therefore sees the wrong cells. Every placement looks like random noise with negative reward, so DONE (reward 0) wins. Fixing how actions line up with cells should be the main lever. I test an explicit horizontal flip of the features before the placement head, the flip with a recipe that gives more samples and more exploration, and a learned per-axis mixing layer that has to discover the mirror itself.

### Round 2
Round 1 shows this world mirrors placements along x. A brick anchored at column x fills columns X-x-dx to X-1-x. Flipping features before the footprint head fixed the collapse to DONE: r1c1 scored 0.745 (0.72, 0.77). r1c3 tried to learn the mirror with linear layers across the axes and failed (0.000), so the flip must be built in. r1c2 (2 epochs, more entropy) got 0.61, but its seeds (0.78, 0.44) are too far apart to call it better or worse. Training success was still rising at the end (0.38 to 0.60), so updates are scarce: the default recipe gives only 30. Failing builds still overlap the target well (IoU 0.96, about 0.46 cells outside per episode). That suggests ordering and landing-layer mistakes. The head's max/min/mean pooling loses which footprint cell is which. Next: a head that keeps each footprint cell, more frequent smaller updates, and both together.

### Round 3
Mirroring the features along x before the footprint head is what made learning possible. Every network without it scored 0, including the learned axial mixing. With the flip in place, the training recipe mattered most. Halving n_envs to 128 doubled the number of updates and raised dev success from 0.745 to 0.888 (r2c2), with the two seeds close together (0.893 and 0.883). The footprint-conv head scored about the same as the pooling head when given the same recipe (0.877 vs 0.888), so the head design is not the bottleneck. Cutting PPO epochs to 2 to get more samples made the results less stable (seeds 0.78 and 0.44). Training success was still rising at the end of r2c2 (0.79 at 75%, 0.86 at 100%), so learning seems limited by the number of updates. The remaining failures are probably about build order (overhangs), which needs more context. This round: push update frequency further, try a higher learning rate, and test a larger receptive field.

### Round 4
The main gain came from flipping the feature map along x so that each anchor logit pools over the cells the brick actually fills. Without it, dev success was 0, and learning the mapping with axial mixing (r1c3) also scored 0. After that fix, the number of updates mattered most. With the same sample budget, dev success went from 0.745 (30 updates) to 0.888 (60) to 0.931 (about 120, n_envs 64), and both seeds of each run stayed close. Changes that cost samples or added instability did not help: the footprint-conv head (about equal), the dilated third conv (0.851) and lr 2e-3 (0.833). Seed noise looks like roughly ±0.03–0.05. The remaining failures are small: IoU is 0.995 and about 0.12 cells per episode land outside the target. n_envs is already at its minimum of 64, so this round halves rollout_len to 8 to double the updates again. It also tests trading one PPO epoch for more samples, and a lower entropy bonus, since evaluation is greedy.

## Trial it ended with
name: flip + 64 envs (more updates)
hypothesis: Same network as r2c2, but n_envs drops 128 to 64 with 16 minibatches of 64 samples. That gives about 120 updates instead of 60 on the same number of samples. r2c2 was still improving and doubling updates gave +14 points, so learning looks limited by updates. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is not above 0.888 by more than about 0.03, or if the seeds diverge, since updates on fewer environments are noisier.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
